n: Ahab reports the events on Carmel to Jezebel, focusing not on the Lord’s fire but on the death of her prophets.

f.g: also, in addition.

n: Jezebel swears an oath to kill Elijah within a day. Interestingly, she sends a warning rather than soldiers—perhaps hoping to drive him away and discredit him.

f.w: So let the gods do to me, and more also
f.g: a standard oath formula: ‘May the gods punish me severely if I fail.’

n: After his great victory, Elijah flees for his life about a hundred miles south to Beersheba, at Judah’s southern edge, and leaves his servant there.

f.g: a town at the southern boundary of Judah; ‘from Dan to Beersheba’ meant the whole land.

n: Alone in the desert under a broom tree, Elijah asks to die. Exhausted and discouraged, he feels he has failed like those before him. Even great prophets experience despair—and God meets them there.

f.g: a desert broom shrub (Hebrew rotem), giving thin shade.

n: While he sleeps, an angel touches him and tells him to eat. God’s first answer to despair is rest and nourishment, not rebuke.
Bread baked on hot stones and a jar of water are waiting at his head. He eats and sleeps again.

f.g: baked on hot stones.
a jar or jug.

n: The angel returns, recognizing that the journey ahead is too much for Elijah on his own strength.

f.g: a heavenly messenger acting on the Lord’s behalf.

n: Strengthened by that food, Elijah travels forty days and nights to Horeb (Mount Sinai). Like Moses, he goes to the mountain of God, fasting forty days—a pattern Jesus would also follow.

f.g: another name for Mount Sinai.
food.

n: At Horeb he spends the night in a cave—perhaps the very cleft where Moses saw the Lord’s glory. The Lord asks him a searching question: “What are you doing here?”

f.g: Hebrew ‘the cave,’ suggesting a known place.

n: Elijah pours out his grievance: he has been zealous for the Lord, Israel has broken its covenant, the prophets are dead, and he alone is left.

f.g: zealous, passionately devoted.

f.w: I, even I only, am left

n: The Lord tells him to stand on the mountain. A violent wind shatters rocks, then an earthquake shakes the ground—but the Lord is not in either. These were the dramatic signs of Sinai.

Then fire—but the Lord is not in it either. Then comes a “still small voice,” a gentle whisper. After the fire of Carmel, God teaches that His most important work is often quiet. Latter-day scripture likewise describes the Spirit as a still, small voice that pierces the soul.

f.g: Hebrew qol demamah daqqah: ‘a sound of thin silence’ or ‘a gentle whisper.’

n: Hearing the voice, Elijah covers his face with his cloak in reverence and steps to the cave’s entrance. The Lord asks again, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

f.w: wrapped his face in his mantle

f.g: a prophet’s outer cloak, later a symbol of his authority.

n: Elijah repeats his complaint word for word. His feelings haven’t changed yet, but the Lord will now give him a new mission.
God’s answer is work to do. He sends Elijah to anoint Hazael as king of Aram (Syria), who would become a scourge on unfaithful Israel.

f.g: set apart by pouring oil; here perhaps meaning to designate or appoint.

n: He is also to anoint Jehu as Israel’s next king and Elisha as his own successor. These were fulfilled partly by Elisha and his disciples.

f.g: ‘God is salvation.’
in your place, as your successor.

n: These three—Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha—would carry out the Lord’s judgments on Baal worship.

f.g: Elisha’s ‘sword’ was mostly his prophetic word.

n: Elijah is not alone after all: the Lord has preserved seven thousand faithful people who never bowed to Baal or kissed his image. God always has a faithful remnant.

f.g: kissing an idol or kissing toward it was an act of worship.

n: Elijah finds Elisha plowing with the last of twelve teams of oxen—a sign of a prosperous family. Throwing his cloak over Elisha was a symbolic call to discipleship and succession.

f.g: twelve pairs, showing the family’s wealth.

n: Elisha asks only to say goodbye to his parents. Elijah’s reply—“Go back; what have I done to you?”—leaves the choice with Elisha. Compare the Savior’s teaching about putting the hand to the plow.

f.w: Let me, I pray thee, kiss my father and my mother

n: Elisha slaughters his oxen, burns his plowing gear to cook them, and feeds the people. With nothing to return to, he follows Elijah and becomes his servant. True discipleship burns the bridges back to the old life.

f.g: the wooden yokes and plow.
served him as an assistant.
